doc.title: David Spinozza interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, NY, September 27, 2025

chapter: Famous sessions and the guitar sound
title: Playing on Don McLean's American Pie
summary: He told McLean to cut verses; with producer John Simon and pianist Paul Griffin, he played on it, a rubato-opening, heavily edited record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: That’s a great story. Did you know when you were playing on a hit?
No. You don’t. In fact I played on “Bye Bye Miss American Pie.”

And it’s really funny because I guess the producer knew that the studio musicians weren’t going to tolerate playing this song over and over again for a lot so he rehearsed Don McLean for weeks by himself with his bass player, and then he called me and Paul Griffin, the piano player, to be the two studio guys on the record. So when we get there we’re running it down, I’ll never forget this, and I say to Don McLean, “You know you really should cut out some verses. This is really too long. This will never get on the radio.” How wrong was I? I said, “You know they only go for two minutes, maybe two- thirty, maybe three minutes on a record, on a 45. This is never going to be on the radio. And the producer, I think John Simon was like, “Shut up, Spinozza, just play the part.” And anyway the rest is history.
And that tune has some odd measures in it every once in a while.

And it also had rubato. Remember it starts like out of time? There was no records that started out of time and then went into time and then went out of time. And that long. That was a rare – how they ended up with airplay on that was amazing.
Do you remember if he sang – the vocal we hear, is that the thing he was singing?

Well he was singing once again what we call it the dummy vocal. He sang live with his playing but then I think he went in and fixed stuff. ‘Cause like we were talking earlier, on a record, you know a record has to last a lot of listens. You can’t have out of tune singing or any of this. So they would go in and fix a lot. Apparently John Simon said there was like 50 edits or something on that record. You don’t hear that but that was a very put together record.
